details:
**Girl with a Pearl Earring**
Vermeer's most famous work (c. 1665), nicknamed the "Mona Lisa of the North" and held in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. It is a tronie (a study of a face or character type, not a commissioned portrait) of a girl in a blue-and-yellow turban who turns over her shoulder toward the viewer against a dark background, showing a large pearl earring. The blue was made from ultramarine (crushed lapis lazuli), and the painting inspired Tracy Chevalier's 1999 novel, in which a Protestant maid named Griet models for the painting.

**The Milkmaid**
Vermeer's painting (c. 1658, Rijksmuseum) of a sturdy kitchen maid in a yellow bodice and blue apron pouring milk from a jug into a bowl beside a basket of bread. A foot warmer sits on the floor behind her in front of Delft tiles, one of which shows Cupid.

**View of Delft**
Vermeer's cityscape (c. 1660–1661, Mauritshuis) of his hometown seen from across the Schie River, with small figures on the near shore, boats in the harbor, and dark clouds casting shadows. Sunlight hits the bell-less tower of the Nieuwe Kerk (New Church), and he mixed sand into the paint for texture. Marcel Proust's character Bergotte dies looking at its "little patch of yellow wall."

**The Art of Painting**
Also called The Allegory of Painting (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna). An artist seen from behind paints a model posing as Clio, the muse of history, who holds a trumpet and a book and wears a laurel wreath. Behind them hang a large map of the Seventeen Provinces of the Netherlands and a chandelier topped with a double-headed Habsburg eagle.

**The Astronomer and The Geographer**
A pair of paintings of scholars, probably modeled by the same man, possibly Vermeer's fellow Delft citizen Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, the pioneer of microscopy, who later served as executor of Vermeer's estate. In The Astronomer, a man in a robe reaches toward a celestial globe beside a book by Adriaan Metius. In The Geographer, a long-haired man holding dividers looks up from a map toward a window. The two canvases were cut from the same bolt of cloth.

**The Concert**
Vermeer's painting of two women, one at a harpsichord and one singing, with a lutenist seen from behind; a copy of Dirck van Baburen's The Procuress hangs on the wall. It was stolen from Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in the 1990 heist and has never been recovered; it is often called the most valuable stolen painting in the world.

**The Allegory of Faith**
A late Vermeer allegory (Metropolitan Museum of Art) of a woman personifying the Catholic faith. She rests her hand on her chest and her foot on a terrestrial globe, gazes up at a glass sphere hanging from the ceiling, and sits in front of a painting of the Crucifixion. Vermeer had converted to Catholicism when he married.

**Window on the left**
A hallmark of Vermeer's quiet domestic interiors: light usually falls into the room from a window on the left side of the picture. Examples include The Geographer, The Milkmaid, and Woman Holding a Balance, while A Lady Writing a Letter is a notable exception.

**Camera obscura**
An optical device that projects an image through a lens or pinhole, which many scholars think Vermeer used to help achieve his precise light effects and soft, blurred highlights. The inventor Tim Jenison argued, in the documentary Tim's Vermeer, that Vermeer used a lens with a "comparator mirror."

**The Love Letter**
A Vermeer painting (Rijksmuseum) viewed through a doorway from a dim hallway with slippers and a broom on the floor, as if intruding on the room. A seated woman holding a cittern (a lute-like instrument) receives a letter from her maid.

**The Music Lesson**
Also called A Lady at the Virginals with a Gentleman (Royal Collection, UK). A young woman stands with her back to the viewer at a virginal (a small keyboard instrument) while a man watches; a viola da gamba lies on a black-and-white tiled floor, and an Oriental rug covers a table in the foreground.

**Woman Holding a Balance**
Vermeer's painting (National Gallery of Art, Washington) of a woman in blue weighing on an empty scale while standing in front of a painting of the Last Judgment. It is often read as a meditation on worldly versus spiritual judgment.

**Théophile Thoré-Bürger**
The French critic who rediscovered Vermeer in the 19th century, after he had largely been forgotten. Writing as "William Bürger," he published influential articles in the Gazette des Beaux-Arts in 1866, attributed many works to Vermeer that had been credited to others, and called him the "Sphinx of Delft."

**Han van Meegeren**
A Dutch forger of the 1930s–40s who painted fake Vermeers, most famously The Supper at Emmaus, which was modeled partly on Caravaggio's painting of the same subject. After selling a forgery to Hermann Göring he was charged with treason, and he proved his innocence by showing he had painted the works himself.

**The Ghost of Vermeer of Delft Which Can Be Used as a Table**
Salvador Dalí's 1934 painting of a dark, Vermeer-like figure kneeling with an extremely long leg that serves as a tabletop. Vermeer's early works include The Procuress, a brothel scene in which the man on the left looking at the viewer may be a self-portrait.
